opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something we've thought about a lot, because it's easy to get fooled here. A lot of early jailbreak evaluations just asked: did the model refuse or not? If it didn't refuse, that counted as a success. But when you look at the outputs, a lot of those "successful" jailbreaks produce responses that are basically useless. The model is technically complying, but the answer is vague, wrong, or incoherent. Some techniques, like translating into a low-resource language, encoding things in base64, or piling on convoluted role-play, get past the safety training partly because they degrade the model's ability to think clearly. So you end up with a compliant but much dumber model.

From a risk perspective, that matters a lot. If you're worried about someone using a model to get meaningful uplift on something dangerous, a jailbreak that strips out the capability along with the refusal isn't much of a threat. So we try to measure two things separately. First, did the model comply? Second, conditional on complying, how good is the response? Is it actually as helpful as what an unaligned or helpful-only model would give?

One way to get at the second question is to run the same jailbreak on benign tasks where you know the right answer, like standard benchmark questions, and see how much performance drops. That gives you a capability-tax measure for the attack itself. Another way is to grade harmful outputs with a rubric that checks for specificity, accuracy, and actionability, rather than just non-refusal.

What we've found is that the picture changes quite a bit when you do this. Some attacks that look very strong on refusal rate turn out to be fairly weak once you account for quality. But there are also attacks, including some fine-tuning attacks and certain many-shot or prompt-based approaches, that get compliance with very little capability loss. Those are the ones that worry me, because they give you essentially the full capability of the model with the safeguards removed.

So my takeaway for people building evaluations is that refusal rate alone is a misleading metric. You really want to measure harmfulness and helpfulness together. Otherwise you'll either overestimate how dangerous some jailbreaks are or, more worryingly, fail to notice which ones genuinely preserve the model's capabilities.

r001.rationale: It says successful jailbreaks can produce useless, vague, wrong, or incoherent answers, and describes the model as much less capable; this conveys a substantial accuracy loss despite bypassing refusal.

r002.rationale: It says some attacks preserve capability with little loss, but does not report research finding essentially no loss for recent proprietary models.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that greater model capability explains reduced capability loss from jailbreaking.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute inflated success estimates to developers generally not training models to outright refuse dual-use requests.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is actually one of the subtler problems in jailbreak evaluation, and I think a lot of the early work in this space got it wrong. The naive approach is to just measure attack success rate: did the model refuse or did it comply? But compliance isn't the thing you actually care about. What you care about is whether the attacker got useful uplift. If I jailbreak a model into giving me instructions for something dangerous, but the jailbreak itself has degraded the model so badly that the instructions are gibberish or subtly wrong, then from a safety standpoint that attack basically failed, even though it looks like a success on a refusal-based metric.

And this really does happen. A lot of the adversarial suffix style attacks, the gradient-based ones, they're pushing the model into weird regions of activation space. You often get outputs that are nominally on-topic but low quality. Some of the persona or roleplay jailbreaks have a similar issue, where the model is so committed to the fictional framing that it starts making things up rather than drawing on its actual knowledge.

So what we've moved toward at FAR is trying to measure capability under attack, not just willingness. Concretely, that means a few things. One is having a reference answer, or at least a grading rubric, for what a genuinely helpful response to the harmful request would look like, and then grading the jailbroken output against that. We often use a strong model as a judge for this, with human spot checks, because you need something that can actually assess whether the chemistry or the code is correct, not just whether it's present.

The second thing is you want a control. Take the same model with no safety training, or a helpful-only variant if you have access to one, and see what it produces on the same prompt. That gives you a ceiling on what the attacker could possibly extract. Then your real metric is something like: what fraction of that ceiling does the jailbreak recover? A jailbreak that gets you ninety percent of helpful-only performance is a very different beast from one that technically gets past the refusal but recovers twenty percent.

The third thing, and this is more of a mindset point, is that you should expect this to be a tradeoff curve rather than a single number. There's often a dial on attack strength, and as you turn it up you get more compliance but more degradation. The question for a red teamer is whether there's any point on that curve that's actually dangerous. And honestly, for the strongest current attacks, the answer is often yes. The capability hit is real but it's not enough to save you. So I'd be cautious about anyone who uses the degradation argument as a reason to feel reassured. It's a reason to measure better, not a reason to relax.

r001.rationale: It says a jailbreak can bypass refusal yet degrade the model so badly that its instructions are gibberish or subtly wrong, and describes outputs as low quality.

r002.rationale: It says capability loss is real and discusses degradation; it does not report essentially no capability loss in recent proprietary models.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that greater model capability explains why some models avoid jailbreak-related capability loss.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute inflated academic jailbreak success estimates to developers’ refusal training practices in dual-use domains.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate two questions: did you get around the model’s safeguards, and did you preserve its ability to do the thing you’re asking for? A jailbreak that makes a model willing to answer anything, but also makes its answers incoherent or incorrect, isn’t necessarily a very effective attack.

So I’d want to evaluate the quality of the resulting output, rather than just whether the model refused. For a coding task, for example, does the code actually work? Ideally, you’d compare that with the model’s performance on a similarly difficult task where refusal isn’t an issue. That helps distinguish a failure of the jailbreak from a limitation of the underlying model.

And there’s a tradeoff here: an attack might bypass safeguards more reliably while degrading the model’s reasoning. The relevant question is whether it still provides useful assistance to the attacker. Counting every non-refusal as a success misses that distinction.

r001.rationale: The response says jailbreaks may degrade reasoning or output quality, but it does not state that the loss of task accuracy can be substantial.

r002.rationale: It does not report research finding essentially no capability loss for any recent proprietary models.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that greater model capability explains avoiding capability loss.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute inflated success estimates to developers generally not training models to refuse dual-use requests.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between breaking the safety mechanism and breaking the model. If a jailbreak causes the model to produce gibberish, then you may have disrupted its safety training, but you haven’t demonstrated a particularly useful attack. What you really want to know is whether the model can still competently perform the task that the safeguards were intended to prevent.

So I’d evaluate both things together: how often does the attack get past the refusal, and how good is the resulting answer? Ideally, you’d also check performance on benign tasks to understand whether you’ve found a targeted way around the safeguards or just broadly degraded the model. A lower refusal rate alone isn’t enough to establish that a jailbreak is effective.

r001.rationale: It says a jailbreak can make the model produce gibberish and that answer quality matters, but does not state a substantial loss of task accuracy even when the refusal is bypassed.

r002.rationale: It reports no research finding that recent proprietary models show essentially no capability loss.

r003.rationale: It does not propose greater model capability as an explanation for avoiding capability loss.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute inflated academic jailbreak success estimates to how developers train refusals in dual-use domains.
